transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-17
Start: 14:30 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Mehta (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Lumina), Evan Cho (Lumina), Dr. Samir Patel (Lumina)

Summary:
Quick, pragmatic smoke profiling session to validate mixed GPU (A100 + H100) inference behavior on Redwood runtime with KV cache persistence, eviction under memory pressure, batching tradeoffs, and comparison notes vs T-R-T-LLM (TensorRT-LLM) and vee-ell-ell-em (vLLM) backends. Action items and pilot next steps captured at end.

Topics covered:
- Heterogeneous GPU setup (nvlink, PCI-e, topology)
- Persistent KV cache impact and cross-socket eviction patterns
- CUDA Graph usage: replay stability when kernels switch
- Batching heuristics vs throughput/latency SLOs
- Quantization artifacts (4-bit vs 8-bit) and kernel selection
- VPC / on-prem networking constraints for private deployment

Notes on artifacts shared: benchmark spreadsheet link (redwood/benchmarks/lumina-smoke-2027-03.xlsx), NVTX trace bundle (s3://redwood-temp/lumina/2027-03/), security checklist (link sent in follow-up).

--- Transcript (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect) ---
[00:00] Jordan: Ok, thanks everyone for hopping on, uh this is Jordan from Redwood, I'll do a quick agenda. Priya is gonna walk through the microbench results we ran overnight and then we'll jump into the KV eviction traces you shared.
[00:18] Priya: Hi all, hey. quick note, we did two runs: pure A100 nodes and mixed A100+H100 where the H100s were used for 2/3 of the batch lanes. Run was with MedicalBERT-7B quantized first to 4-bit, then 8-bit to look at kernel selector changes.
[00:36] Marta: Quick question on that, is the quant a post-training q or is it PTQ + some rounding? We need to know bc for certs the reproducibility matters.
[00:50] Priya: It's PTQ with a small calibration set, we used the usual symmetric quant and tuned the zero-point a bit; some ops fell back to fp16 kernels on the TRT path. The vLLM runs used their int8 path where possible.
[01:10] Evan: Sorry, quick infra note — our cluster is heterog, one rack A100, one rack H100, connected via NVLink within racks and PCI-e across racks. We don't have a shared NVLink across all GPUs.
[01:27] Priya: That topology matters because we saw cross-socket KV cache misses that caused memory eviction thrash when the runtime tried to pull KV pages across PCI-e.
[01:43] Dr. Samir: Can you explain the eviction pattern again? We had an earlier hypothesis that persistent KV would reduce repeated re-encoding.
[01:52] Priya: Yes so persistent KV helps warm prefixes, but on mixed GPUs the runtime chooses kernel paths differently per device. On H100 the kernel prefers the TRT-optimized fused attention, while on A100 it picked an alternative kernel. That mismatch changes the memory working set and under sustained batched traffic we saw the KV pages get pushed out then pulled back, extra PCI-e transfers, which spiked tail latency.
[02:20] Jordan: And this was most evident with larger batch coalescing, right?
[02:24] Priya: Exactly. At batch sizes above 8 the CUDA-graph replay sometimes replayed a different kernel path than recorded because the kernel selector did dynamic decisions at runtime — cooda-graph replay instability. That caused a fallback and recompile path on TRT-LLM in one of our tests.
[02:46] Marta: So is that a TRT-LLM specific issue or also seen with vLLM?
[02:52] Priya: Both. Different failure modes: TRT-LLM was tripped by graph replay mismatch when quantized fused ops were present and cudagraph replay assumed fixed kernel IDs. vLLM had more dynamic dispatch but incurred higher per-token CPU overhead in our test, more context-switching, which impacted throughput but showed fewer hard fallbacks.
[03:18] Evan: We also saw that under a network hiccup the persistent KV unserialized to disk which amplified IOPS — is that something you saw?
[03:27] Priya: Yeah, when the runtime flushes to disk due to memory pressure we noticed I/O spikes; on our on-prem setup that saturated the local NVMe and created queuing delays. On cloud-hosted Redwood we can keep KV in GPU memory more aggressively with eviction heuristics, but in private VPC/on-prem you need to size local NVMe and set eviction thresholds more conservatively.
[03:52] Jordan: Can we walk through the raw numbers you ran overnight? Priya, you have the quick table?
[03:58] Priya: Sure. For A100-only: median latency 45ms @ batch=4, 1200 tokens/sec throughput @ 4-bit quant; for mixed A100+H100: median 38ms @ batch=4, 1600 tokens/sec throughput but 99th latency regressed under sustained runs to ~420ms when KV thrash started. TRT path had slightly lower median but higher worst-case when recompile happened. vLLM had stable tails around 220ms but lower mean throughput.
[04:34] Marta: The 99th to 420ms is concerning for our SLOs, we need <250ms 95th.
[04:41] Priya: Agreed — that's where policy routing helps. Redwood runtime can route high-priority traffic to dedicated lanes pinned on homogeneous H100 pools to avoid cross-device kernel divergence. That is more a Dedicated capacity play.
[05:00] Dr. Samir: Did you test with prefix caching enabled and disabled? Because some of our traffic has long prefixes.
[05:08] Priya: Yes; prefix caching reduced token generation by ~11% on average but increased memory pressure. We recommend a mixed strategy: KV caching for the hottest prefixes with eviction TTLs, plus per-request short-term in-memory cache for mid-tier prefixes.
[05:27] Evan: From network side, if we keep the KV pinned to GPUs we need to ensure our VPC setup allows cross-subnet low-latency paths, else we'll see PCI-e fallbacks. We'll send a topology.
[05:38] Jordan: On the CUDA graph front, what's the remediation? Re-recording per-batch-size? Fixed kernel map?
[05:45] Priya: A couple layers: 1) prefer deterministic kernel selector at record time (disable some adaptive heuristics), 2) record multiple graphs for common bucket sizes and select at replay time, 3) for TRT use a hybrid strategy where if graph replay mismatch is detected we fallback to vLLM-like dynamic path instead of triggering heavy recompile. We prototyped this third option during the run and it prevented the 3-5s recompile spike but cost some steady-state throughput.
[06:18] Marta: On quantization fidelity — any observed regression on clinical prompt outputs? We need minimal semantic drift.
[06:25] Priya: For 4-bit PTQ we observed small hallucination increases on long-context summarization prompts, 8-bit was much closer to fp16. For strict quality we recommend 8-bit or mixed quant with activation-aware fallback on critical ops.
[06:40] Dr. Samir: Noted. Could we also get a sample diff of model outputs between fp16 and 4-bit for our evaluation set?
[06:47] Jordan: Yes we'll attach delta outputs to the benchmark spreadsheet.
[06:50] [07:00] Speaker 1: (someone in background) can you put those numbers in the doc?
[07:06] Jordan: Will do.
[07:10] Priya: One more behavior we saw — the runtime's kernel mapper tends to favor TRT fused attention on H100 which improves latency when sequence lengths are short, but when sequence length grows the kernel switches to a slower memory-friendly algorithm which increases resident set size and triggers eviction.
[07:32] Evan: Is there a knob to force kernel choice?
[07:36] Priya: Yes, at the runtime config level you can pin execution policy per model version. We can propose safe defaults for your pilot.
[07:44] Marta: Security question — if we move to Redwood private, how does KV encryption at rest work? Our compliance wants KMS/HSM and audit logs.
[07:53] Jordan: For Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM, KV at rest is encrypted using your key; audit logs are exported to your SIEM. We'll send SOC2/ISO artifacts.
[08:05] Marta: Good. Also need RBAC for developers vs product vs infra.
[08:10] Jordan: Console supports token-scoped roles and SAML SSO, can provide RBAC mapping suggestions.
[08:16] Priya: Back to perf — we also tried mixed batching heuristics: adaptive batching with latency SLO target and fixed-size batching. Adaptive kept median low but produced tail variance; fixed-size gave more predictable tails at cost of throughput. For your 95th <250ms target we'd recommend fixed-size lanes for high-priority traffic and an adaptive lane for best-effort.
[08:44] Evan: Any special notes about on-prem NVMe sizing?
[08:48] Priya: Rule of thumb from our test: if >50% of your traffic uses persistent KV then aim for NVMe bandwidth of at least 10 GB/s sustained and headroom for random writes. Otherwise you'll see queueing during eviction.
[09:03] Dr. Samir: Regarding TRT recompile — what causes that to kick in? Is it new kernel selection at replay time?
[09:10] Priya: Exactly — if the recorded graph references kernel A but runtime decision picks kernel B for a particular device shape/quant, TRT's graph replay may fail and trigger a recompile. We saw that when mixed precisions were present across devices.
[09:29] Marta: Ok can you summarize recommended pilot config?
[09:33] Jordan: We'll propose a 3-week pilot: week 0 setup + baseline (benchmarks); week 1 stress tests and tail analysis; week 2 optimizations (pinning, kernel maps, eviction thresholds). Priya will run the initial heterog microbench. We also want to validate security docs and finalize model/prompt set.
[09:54] Priya: For the pilot baseline we'll collect: per-token latency histograms, NVTX traces, kernel selection logs, CUDA graph record+replay diffs, and model output diffs (fp16 vs 8-bit vs 4-bit).
[10:10] Evan: we'll also provide topology and sample traffic traces.
[10:13] Jordan: Great. Any other questions?
[10:16] Marta: One last proc question — does Redwood have a built-in cost knob to route to lower-cost lanes when tails spike?
[10:24] Priya: Not automated cost-swap today, but you can configure routing policies by latency tiers + model variants; Redwood Optimize can recommend when to quantize or route to lower-cost model variants. We'll include cost estimates in the spreadsheet.
[10:40] Dr. Samir: Are there known incompatibilities with certain kernel fusion patterns and model architectures?
[10:46] Priya: Sparse attention and some custom causal masking patterns triggered non-fused fallbacks in TRT; we documented those in the notes.
[10:55] Jordan: Ok we should wrap. Quick recap of next steps: Jordan share sheet, Priya run microbench, Evan share network/topology, Lumina confirm model/prompt set, schedule pilot kickoff.
[11:11] Marta: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

End of call.
